# aarne-petrie-flexheg-part-iii-2025
- **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15100 (PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.15100, 59 pp., text extracted locally; printed page = PDF page) · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v2→v3 response round, slice N (item N3b)
- **What it establishes:** flexHEG Part III has a dedicated section on consumer GPUs — but its heading is "Consumer GPUs Could Likely be Exempted" and its conclusion is AGAINST restrictions on consumer GPUs. It contemplates, without endorsing, adding flexHEG to the most powerful consumer chips; conditions exemption on "reasonable efforts" to limit large-scale usefulness and stockpiling; and in footnote 6 floats a "small tax on generality" pushing consumer AI chips toward console-like lockdown. So the paper considers consumer devices in scope of the design conversation, yet recommends exempting them.
- **Key passages:**
  - p. 18, section "Consumer GPUs Could Likely be Exempted": "A key question would be whether powerful consumer chips would be exempted altogether, subjected to some form of registration and oversight requirements, or whether the sale of powerful AI-relevant chips to consumers would be banned altogether. How consumer chips would be handled will depend on specific risk assessments and policy goals, but it appears likely that they can simply be exempted, as long as some reasonable efforts are made to limit these chips' usefulness for large-scale computing applications, and to block any one actor from stockpiling them for use in clusters."
  - p. 18, fn. 5: "If necessary, consumer GPU distributors might also be randomly asked to provide documentation to verify that a random sample of their chips were indeed sold to ordinary consumers."
  - p. 19: "In this case it may seem appealing to add some version of flexHEG to some of the most powerful consumer chips, as a protection against malicious use, and use as large clusters. However, most of the plausible malicious use prevention mechanisms we discuss below would be relatively poorly suited to applications in consumer chips. Even more importantly, it would likely become impractical to recall existing uncontrolled stocks of consumer GPUs. ... Therefore the advantages of restrictions on consumer GPUs would likely fail to justify their administrative costs and negative impacts on trade and compute access."
  - p. 19, fn. 6 (complete): "One low cost practical approach could be to incentivize most consumer AI chips to be configured to have relatively limited capabilities, such as current video game consoles, which make it difficult to run arbitrary software. This could take the form of a small tax on generality or e.g. high-bandwidth networking capabilities. If most users' needs fall within a limited scope, this could be a way to ensure that most newly produced, widely available chips would be difficult to misuse, hampering malicious actors' stockpiling efforts at only limited cost to legitimate users."
  - p. 16 lists as an open design question: "Would carve-outs be needed for special cases, such as consumer GPUs"
- **Reliability:** Primary; arXiv preprint of a report commissioned by ARIA (dated April 2025 on its cover; arXiv submission 18 June 2025). Not peer-reviewed.
- **Relevance to this project:** The review OVER-REACHES if it says the essay's sentence is simply "false" for Part III: the main text recommends exemption. What is true: Part III does not "expressly" design for datacenters only — it treats consumer chips as a live question, makes exemption conditional, and its footnote 6 proposes a tax on general-purpose consumer compute, which is directly relevant to the essay's general-purpose-computing theme. Citation: Onni Aarne and James Petrie, "Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees, Part III: International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees" (report dated April 2025), arXiv:2506.15100 (18 June 2025) — arXiv title: "International Security Applications of Flexible Hardware-Enabled Guarantees." Two authors only.
